Annemarie Clark-Schwarzenbach:
IRAN UNDERNAY

When some three years ago the name of the old Persian Monarchy
was officially changed into Iran this was but a symbol of the national
renaissance which, during the eleven years of the reign of H. M. Reza Shah
Pehlevi has been watched by the entire world with surprise and admiration.

During and since the World War far off Persia has been
involved in a movement toward nationalism, secularism, and a process of
econemic changes, caused,[sic] in the near East partly by the breaking off of the
Ottoman Empire: Pan-Islamism giving way to strong nationalistic movements;
partly by the fact that the European powers after the collapse of Russian
and German Imperialism went in for a new policy of trade agreements and
econemic control rather than return to the political, military and colonial
methods that had been usual up to the war.

Before and during the war, the weakness of the old Persian
Government had become more and more obvious and had converted Persia into
a veritable battlefield for the European powers and European as well as
Turkish armies. The Czarists maintained Cossack regiments in the northern
part of the country, with permanent garrisons in northern provincial towns,
such as Rescht, Kasvin, etc. The British had influence Muzaffer od Din
Schah as early as 1906 to grant a constitution which could have changed the
government into a sort of limited monarchy with the newly founded Majlis
acting as a parliament. But the next Shah, Mohamed Ali, in League with the
Czarists, bombarded the Majlis and abolished the new constitution. He was
posed, thanks partly to British diplomatic activity, and his infant son,
Sultan Ahmed, placed on the throne with Nassar ul Mulk as Regent. Persia,
though formerly independent, was in fact divided into two zones, that of
Russian and that of British influence.

During the war it became apparent that Persia was not
capable of depending its neutrality against invasions by Germans, Turks,
Russians, and finally the English. German agents such as Wasmuth and
Niedermayer succeeded in rousing the Nomad tribes in Luristan and elsewhere.
[add inline: The] Curzon-Cox agreement of 1919, brought forward by the British, would have
put Persia into a position of tutelage, the British acquiring financial and
military control in return for a loan.

But the agreement was never ratified by the Majlis and mean
while the Bolsheviks invaded the province of Gilan on the shores of the
Caspian Sea and were on their way to Teheran. Assisted by British troups,
the Persians kept the Russians back, but at this moment a military conspiracy
was hatched at Kasvin in the midst of the English headquarter. A Persian
officer, formerly of one of the Russian Persian Cossac regiments, Reza Kahan,
marched on Teheran with 3000 men, which was forced[add above: forcing it] to capitulate. A govern
ment under the Seyid was set up by Reza, he himself first acting only as
military Governor of Teheran, but soon becoming Minister of War. The "March
on Teheran" of February 1921 about simultaneous with the national uprising
of Kemal Pascha in Turkey, and preceeding Mussolini's famous march on Rome
is the beginning of a new period in the history of Persia.

Soon after the capitulation of Teheran, the Seyid was turned
out of the country, and the Shah no longer feeling secure in his own capital
fled to Paris and refused to return. Resa Kahan, by this time Prime Minister,
finally declared himself Shah and was crowned as Reza Shah Pahlavi[add above: Pehlevi] on
October 21, 1925.

The abolishment of foreign capitulation was the first and most
important step toward political independence and the establishment of a
nationalistic state. But the Shah, like Kemal Pascha, strongly influenced

by the example of Turkey, saw the necessity of adapting the country to modern
conditions in order to make its political independance effective.
This meant first economic change from a purely agrarian to an industrial
order, built up on the natural resources of the country; but it also necessitated
total regeneration of the Persian or Jran people to make them capable of adapting
themselves to an entirely new course.

The example of modern Turkey, called in pre-war diplomatic language
"the Invalid of the Bosporus", has proved wrong the western conception of the near
East as a degenerate part of the world, exhausted by its early accomplished
historical task, unable to take any produktive[sic] part in the course of present day
events. Jt is easy to establish the parallels between Turkey and Jran, Turkey acting
as leader in the movement of national recovery which involved also Egypt, Jrak, Afgha
nistan, and, to a certain degree, Syria and Palestine. But in order to understand what
is going on in modern Jran, it is important to state that Persia has its own and
different historical background, and was, at the moment of the "March on Teheran", in
a position entirely different from the rest of the near East. Persia did not at any
period belong to the Ottoman Empire, and it never took part in the so-called
Arabian world. Persia[add above: It] was not as strongly involved in the political game of
Pan-Jslamism which was one of the important factors in the recent uprising of the
pre-war imperialism as Turkey had been. Persia was an almost forgotten country
until its oilfields were discovered by William Knox d'Arcy, who secured himself
in 1901 an exclusive concession for the whole country excepting the five Northern
Provinces bordering the Caspian Sea. This concession, originally granted for 60
years, has undergone many changes, resulting finally in the monopoly of the Anglo-
Jranian Oil Company.

As for the religious question, since the majority of Persians
belong to the Shiah sect which is detested by the Sunnis, they have a place
apart in the near East, and certainly have nothing in common with the partly
nationalistic and racial and partly religious movement which shakes most of
the Islamic world today. There are quite a number of Christians living mostly
in the north besides a number of Jewish and Zoroastirian communities.

During the World War Persia not only suffered from the weakness
its own government, it also suffered from a general lack of unity and
national feeling. The tribes were easily stirred up against the rest of the
country, and the Christian population in Azerbeidjan was persccuted by Kurdish
and fanatic Moslems. The "March on Teheran" certainly was not a symbolic
action expressing an inevitable national uprising against the foreign armies
invading the country; it was the action of a single man, [add above: a*]purely military
event and it is only natural that the army has remained a unit of the
greatest importance, in the new government finding some most devoted
supporters among the officers. The Shah is first and foremost a soldier, –
and his idea of regeneration has been to use the army for this purpose, an
army strong enough to turn Turkish bandits, German agents and Bolshevik
invaders out of the country.

The result of this [add above: The next step*] has been the pacification and unification
of the country carried out successfully though with much brutality, – and
here again the army was the one instrument in the hand of Reza Shah Pehlevi
whose government could therefore, at least at the beginning, be called a
Military dictatorship. Without the surprising action of the Shah, there
would have been not only a very possible danger from Bolshevistik propaganda
but very probably description in the[add above: into] tribunal unity to handle by whoever
might want to get foothold in Persia.

Furthermore, unification and the establishment of a strong
and centralized government was the one condition under which to start any
effective changes in a country which for centuries had been out of contact
with the Western World and kept back politically and economically in a
medieval state. If the action of the soldier Reza Kahan did not coincide
with a strong national feeling of the whole country, it certainly opened the
way to a national regeneration on a progressive line. There existed,
throughout the country, a number of broad-minded, liberal and well educated
men who realized the opportunity given to their country and joined the
new Shah in his aim to acquire not only political independence but also
collaborated in adapting the social and economic conditions of Persia to
modern standards. Reforms in Persia (now officially called Iran) owe much
to such man as Taimurtash who was popular in foreign diplomatic circles and
died in prison after one of his race horses had beaten a horse of the Shah's
stable in a Teheran race.

True, there is still antagonism between the reforms rapidly
carried out through a minority of progressive-minded men, imposed by a
powerful government, – and the majority of Persian people, thinly scattered
over a big area of half desert land, accustomed to poverty and hunger,
uneducated, mostly illiterate, and not knowing what is going on about them.
They do understand that there is now compulsory military service which they
try to escape. They do know that they are supposed to abandon their old
costumes and wear curious European clothes and hats which they don't like
and which make them look ridiculous. The Nomad tribes, most of them belonging
to the Turkish race speaking Turkish dialects, are forced by the Teheran
government to settle down, to live in houses instead of black tents, and to
give up their independence.

Control of the tribunal and nomadic population was essential
to the carrying out military service, taxation and jurisdiction. It has
stopped the bandits, until then frequently robbing, kidnapping and killing
travelers; whereas now travelling security is guaranteed; police guards have
been established along the roads and travelling is safe even through such
remote countries as Luristan, formerly notorious for its ruthless mountaineer
bands. The Lurs, after several uprisings as recent as 1932 against the new
government have finally been partly supported[ev. meint sie hier eher: deported, siehe auch nächster Absatz], partly settled in villages.
Deportation of Lurs and in smaller number also of Kurdisch[sic] tribunal peoples
from the region of Hamadan have been very cruel as the deported were given no
opportunity to become acclimatised to their new surroundings and many died
during the transport.

The Turkish-speaking tribes of Kashgais ane Bakhtiaris living
in the mountains parts of middle and south Persia gave the most serious
treuble. However, they stopped resistance after some of their chiefs were
summoned to Teheran and executed. A similar process was used against the
rich lands, who are heavily taxed. The existing agrarian system, namely
the division of territory into big properties with peasants or tenants or wage
workers has not been changed. But in many cases the landlord were accused
of not paying their taxes. Sumsened to the capital they were practically
forced to remain as prisoners in their own town houses and their property was
confiscated by the government and converted into private property of the Shah.
Today Reza Shah Pehlavi is the biggest land owner of the country.

Some opposition also came from the Mullahs, a very corrupt and
low class of Moslem priest, who strongly influenced public life being teachers
of the Mosque schools, – the only existing schools aside from occasional
American, English and French Missionary schools. The tendency toward secularism

in modern Iran is not due to anti-religious motives but the Mullahs being
extremely reactionary and opposed to the progressive line of the government
went on stirring up public opinion and therefore had to be held in check.
The tragic events of last[unclear][add above: the] summer, 1935, then hundreds of people demonstrating
the abolition of the "Shador" (the woman's veil) were killed in the
courtyard of the sanctuary of Meshed, showed that the dangerous influence of
Mullahs still exists. There is much religious fanaticism mixed with
strong conventionality and opposition to a government which, although
sincerely progressive, still bears many features of Asiatic despotism founded
on the power of one strong warrior ruler.

But the determined breaking down of opposition of any kind
doubtless opened the way on which Iran is proceeding to develop rapidly into
a modern country.

The foreign traveler first will recognize not only the
security of practically all parts of Iran, even as remote as the valley of
Luristan, but also the improvement of roads and bridge and the alteration
in the means of transportation produced in the short ten years of the Shah's
actual regime.

Before his reign there were only a few hundred miles of road
open to wheeled traffic but as early as 1931 as many as approximately 6000
miles of motor roads have been constructed. Motor transport is devloping
rapidly although in the mountainous regions pack animals remain the only
means of conveyance, and camel caravans are still used all over the country.
Improved transportation is one of the most urgent needs, considering that
Iran until today has no regular connection, railway or airlines, to the rest
othe world, with the exception of the Persian Gulf port Bushira, reached
by the Indian line of the Dutch K. L. M. and French airline, – and the

Caspian Sea port Pehlevi, connected to Baku by a regular service of the Russian
company "Kaspar". Baghdad may be reached in a three day's motor car drive.
The Trans-Jranian Railway, going from now under construction [add above: and partly completed], will is to go from
Bander Shah on the Caspian Sea to Bender Shahpur on the Persian Gulf. This tremendous
enterprise in carried out by various European companies under control of the skan
dinavian Kampsax Company. A large number of European engeneers[sic - engineers], skilled workmen and
even unskilled laborers are employed at different sections of the railway-con
truction.

The strategic purpose of the railway has been much discussed, as it does'nt touch
Baghdad and therefore fails to connect Jran with the already established airlines,
ailway- and motor-road-traffic leading to the Mediterranean. Jf the Jranian Govern
ment did not plan to connect Teheran either with Jrak or with Jndia, it looks as if
did not want the railway to serve possible British purposes, – but as the rail
way is now debouching on the Turkman border of the Caspian, it consequently is at
the mercy of Soviet Russia.

But this certainly is no actual menace, as since the war the Sovjets seemed to
have abandoned the old Czarist game of absorbing northern Persia, being too busy
with their troubles in the Far East. The most important task of the Trans-Jranian-
Railroad will be to connect the Caspian region with Teheran and the local markets.
The Shah gives special attention to this reg includes the two richest pro
vinces of Jran: Mazanderan and Gilan. Separated from the Jran Highland by the Elburz
Mountainrange, it looked upon Russia as its natural outlet and had but little trade
with the rest of Persia, – to-day[sic] the two Elburz mountain passes of Firuzkuh and
Kasvin have been improved, and a new one, the famous Schalus road, has been constru
ed, leading to the new Caspian port, Deno. The increased traffic and easier access
to the Caspian facilitate trade commercial and cultural relations with Soviet Russia.
The caviar fisheries of the Caspian littoral are generated by an Jrano-Russian
company, rice and cotton, grown in the tropical Mazanderan, are exported to Russia,
cheap Russian goods are purchased in the Persian bazaars, Russian tradesmen have
settled in the northern towns of Rescht, Karvin, Kasvin, Pehlevi, etc. The best hospital in
Teheran, and one of the larger schools, have been established by the Russians. The
Russian language is frequently spoken, in the 2 movie theaters of Teheran captions

are given both in Russian and Persian, less frequently in French or English.
The Russio-Iranian bank in Teheran was established as early as 1925 with
an authorized capital of five million gold rubels and its head office in
Moscow. Russia figures second after Great Britian in the Persian export
scale. Statistics show that woolen, opium, dried fruit, cotton and
rice are the most important export products; except in the case of the rugs
all of these products are agriculturel; opium with around seventy million
being far ahead. Cutting down opium and replacing it by other crops
such as cacoon silk cotton is therefore a difficult vegetarian[?] problem
which keeps the the Opium Commitees of the League of Nations busy and which
might lead to a research of Iran's economic possibilities such as the
exploitation of its mineral resources and building up Industries on this
basis. The government is encouraging private industrial enterprise, sugar
and cement factories and the cotton mill in Shiraz are a promising beginning
in the use of the country's own raw material for local industry.
[p]Finances have been completely reorganized and based on a
two-budget system by Dr. Millsbaugh, American financial expert, who during
a period of 100 of five years acted as Financial Administrator in Iran. The National
Bank of Iran established in 1927 with a capital of two million toman, and its
branch, the cultural Bank of Iran, established in 1930 with a capital of
five million toman, carry on the financial operations for state and government.
One of the most important budgetary revenues is from the royallties and
taxation paid by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company which in 1935 amounted to
[add inline: Pfundzeichen] [illegible] 2,191,921. The concession granted to the company covers 250,000 square
miles situated southwest from a line roughly running through Kermanshah and
through Isfahan. This concession will be reduced to 100,000 square miles
by the end of 1938, the area to be chosen by the company itself, which is
therefore carrying out careful research work throughout the country. Today

the A. I. O. C employs about 25,000 lranian subjects, – skilled workmen and
employees formerly introduced from India are being rapidly replaced by well
trained Iranians. Since oil is the richest natural resource of Iran, it might
have a great effect in the rapid development towards a new industrial order.
The royalties paid by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. are not included in the export
figures of the statistics of foreign trade, but are used in a special Government
budget for such expenditures as the construction of the railway. But in spite
of its budgetary importance, the oil concession granted to the A. I. O. C.
means that the richest and by far the most important and promises resource of
the country of Iran will, for another fifty years, be exploited by a foreign
power. Even if by then, Iran should be able to take over its own Oil industry
Iran Oil still will be at the mercy of the British, who control the Suez-Canal,
and by means of taxation can play on the competition of Iran Oil and the Mosul
oil with its pipe-line running across the Syrian desert down to Haifa and Tri
polis.
Intellectual transformation.
[p]Under whatever angle one chooses to look at modern Iran, the
picture is difficult to visualize. As far as economics are concerned, we so
rapid industrial development, efforts towards a balance budget, and increased
foreign and local trade. But until today no definite plan, considerable to the
turkish five-year-plan has been adopted, and however industrial enterprise is
ebing encourag by the Government, it still depends to a large extent on private
capital and privat initiative, A[sic] complete plan of research as to the fundamen
tal possibilities of raw materials, agricultural production, markets, and trans
portation would be necessary to enable industry and agriculture to colaborate in
converting Iran into an economic organism. However, what has been accomplished
proves the tendency of the Iran Government towards what might be called
"economic nationalism", in order to complete the political independence and
internal security guaranteed by the Shahs' army.

Much has also been done in the field of education, hygiene,
building, and intellectual progress of all kinds. Formerly only boys, trained in
mosque schools (most of them to become priests) or in foreign missionary schools
were able to read or write, but during the past ten years literacy has increased
enormously. Schools are established not only in the larger towns, but in remote
villages, boy students throughout the country wear the same kind of uniforms in
plein gray material. In the girls' schools – which of course are an innovation – the stu
ents are not allowed to wear the veil, or "shador": as girl-scouts, with hair cut short
trained in all kinds of sports, they will forget the old custom which kept the woman
strictly in the house. – About 500 young men are beeing trained in European and Ameri
can schools at Government expense. Foreign professors teach at the University of
Teheran, whos adviser, Professor Haas, is a German refugee. Scouting and sport are en
aged by the Government providing vast playgrounds.

A French military mission helps train the young officers of the army, – which actually
may amount to some 100 000 men, – also exact figures are not available. Some Belgian
officers teach the air force how to handle its fifty air-planes.

The Shah himself does not like to leave the country, and has never been in Europe,
his last official trip beeing limited by[add above: to*] a visit said to Kemal Pascha in Angora.
But his young son recently presented to the army and the Diplenatic Corps in Teheran
was educated in Lausanne (Switzerland) and might stand as an example for the
young Jranians.

Oil, industrialisation, increasing economic wealth are the one con
dition on which to build the national future of Jran; – the other is to overcome
the still existing antagonism due to the rapid and revolutionary changes forced
all too suddenly upon the Jranian people. How the young generation will make use
of the opportunity given to it and undergoe a spiritual transformation, will
determin the course of the new Jran.
